about.title: Berkeley Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Berkeley's workforce is unusually varied for a city of about 121,000 people. Lab technicians, restaurant staff along Shattuck, delivery drivers threading University Avenue, construction crews on housing projects near Ashby, and contractors serving the campus all clock in here every day, and any of them can be hurt on the job. When that happens, California's workers' compensation system usually stands in for a lawsuit against your employer. It pays medical care and partial wages without asking who was at fault, but it also caps what you can recover. What many injured Berkeley workers do not realize is that a separate claim may exist when someone other than the employer caused the harm: a subcontractor who left a hazard, a property owner who ignored a defect, a manufacturer whose tool failed, or another motorist. In 2025 Berkeley recorded 603 injury collisions, and employees who drive for work on I-80 or city streets share those same roads. We review both workers' compensation and third-party injury claims directly with you.

items.title: Two Claims, Not One
items.desc: Workers' compensation is usually your only remedy against your employer, but a negligent subcontractor, property owner, equipment maker, or driver can be held separately responsible. We can tell you whether both tracks are open to you.

items.title: Deadlines That Do Not Wait
items.desc: California asks you to report a job injury to your employer within 30 days, and third-party injury claims carry a two-year filing window. Getting in touch early keeps both clocks from running out on you.

items.title: Protection From Pushback
items.desc: It is illegal for an employer to punish you for reporting an injury or filing a claim. If you are worried about your job, we can explain your rights before you speak up.

items.question: I deliver for a Berkeley restaurant and was hit on University Avenue during a Friday evening run. Who covers my injuries?
items.answer: If you were working at the time, your employer's workers' compensation coverage should apply regardless of who caused the crash. Because another driver may have been at fault, you might also have a separate personal injury claim against that driver, which can cover losses workers' comp does not. Friday late afternoons are when Berkeley collision reports tend to cluster, so this scenario is more common than people think. We can review both options with you.

items.question: Can I sue my employer directly for a workplace injury in California?
items.answer: In most cases, no. Workers' compensation is the exclusive remedy against your employer, which means you receive benefits without proving fault but generally cannot file a lawsuit against the company itself. The exception is when a third party, such as a subcontractor or equipment manufacturer, contributed to your injury. That claim proceeds separately.

items.question: What happens if I waited too long to tell my employer about my injury?
items.answer: California asks workers to report an injury to their employer within 30 days, and waiting longer can complicate your workers' compensation claim. It does not automatically end your options, though, and a third-party injury claim runs on its own two-year deadline. Reach out as soon as you can so we can assess where you stand.
